This vignette shows the basic workflow of the package with monthly data from
a single weather station:

1. compute the potential evapotranspiration (PET);
2. compute the climatic water balance, precipitation minus PET;
3. compute the Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI)
   and the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) at several time scales;
4. plot the results and extract the values.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(SPEI)
```

## The data

The `wichita` dataset holds monthly climate records for Wichita, Kansas
(37.6475° N, 402.6 m above sea level) from January 1980 to October 2011.

```{r}
data(wichita)
head(wichita)
```

Precipitation (`PRCP`) is in mm, and temperatures (`TMAX`, `TMIN`, `TMED`) in
°C. The other columns are the mean wind speed (`AWND`), sunshine duration
(`TSUN`) and cloud cover (`ACSH`), which only the Penman method needs. See
`?wichita` for details.

The functions of the package work best with time series (`ts`) objects,
because the dates of the series are then known. We convert the data to a
monthly time series starting in January 1980:

```{r}
wichita <- ts(wichita[, -c(1, 2)], start = c(1980, 1), frequency = 12)
```

## Potential evapotranspiration

The SPEI is based on the climatic water balance, so we first need the PET.
The package has three methods, which need different data:

| Function | Data needed |
|---|---|
| `thornthwaite()` | mean temperature and latitude |
| `hargreaves()` | maximum and minimum temperature and latitude (or extraterrestrial radiation); optionally precipitation |
| `penman()` | maximum and minimum temperature, latitude and elevation, plus wind speed and radiation or a proxy for it (sunshine hours, cloud cover) |

```{r}
lat <- 37.6475

pet_tho <- thornthwaite(wichita[, "TMED"], lat)
pet_har <- hargreaves(wichita[, "TMIN"], wichita[, "TMAX"], lat = lat)
pet_pen <- penman(wichita[, "TMIN"], wichita[, "TMAX"], wichita[, "AWND"],
  tsun = wichita[, "TSUN"], lat = lat, z = 402.6, na.rm = TRUE
)
```

`penman()` needs `na.rm = TRUE` here because wind speed and sunshine duration
have some missing months. The result is in mm per month, and it is a time
series with the same dates as the input:

```{r, fig.alt = "Monthly PET at Wichita from 2000 to 2004 by the Thornthwaite, Hargreaves and Penman methods"}
pet <- cbind(Thornthwaite = pet_tho, Hargreaves = pet_har, Penman = pet_pen)
plot(window(pet, start = c(2000, 1), end = c(2004, 12)),
  plot.type = "single", col = 1:3, ylab = "PET (mm)"
)
legend("topleft", colnames(pet), col = 1:3, lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

The methods follow the same seasonal cycle but differ in magnitude. In
Wichita, the mean annual PET is about 830 mm with Thornthwaite, 1,220 mm with
Hargreaves and 1,490 mm with Penman. Thornthwaite's method uses mean
temperature only, and gives almost no PET in the cold months. Penman's method
is physically based and is the most accurate when the data are available;
Hargreaves' method is a common alternative when only temperature is
available. The Penman series also has gaps where wind or sunshine data are
missing. The choice of PET method affects the SPEI, so it is worth reporting.

Here we use the Hargreaves PET, which needs no missing-data handling:

```{r}
bal <- wichita[, "PRCP"] - pet_har
```

## Computing the SPEI

`spei()` takes the water balance and the time scale, in months. The time
scale is the number of months over which the balance is accumulated: SPEI-1
reflects the conditions of a single month, while SPEI-12 reflects the
conditions of the previous year.

```{r}
spei1 <- spei(bal, 1)
spei3 <- spei(bal, 3)
spei12 <- spei(bal, 12)
```

For each calendar month, the function fits a log-Logistic distribution to the
accumulated balances and converts each value to the standard normal scale.
The result is an object of class `spei`:

```{r}
spei12
```

The first 11 values of SPEI-12 are `NA`, because 12 months are needed for the
first accumulated value.

## Plotting

The `plot()` method shows positive (wet) values in blue and negative (dry)
values in red:

```{r, fig.alt = "Bar plots of SPEI-1 and SPEI-12 at Wichita, 1980-2011, wet months in blue and dry months in red"}
plot(spei1, main = "Wichita, SPEI-1")
plot(spei12, main = "Wichita, SPEI-12")
```

Short time scales vary quickly from month to month, like soil moisture or
river flow in small catchments. Long time scales change slowly and show
long dry or wet periods, like groundwater or reservoir storage. The drought
of 2011 in Kansas shows clearly at the 12-month scale.

## Reading the values

The SPEI is a standardized variable, with mean 0 and standard deviation 1
over the series. A common classification of the values is:

| SPEI | Category |
|---|---|
| 2 or more | extremely wet |
| 1.5 to 2 | severely wet |
| 1 to 1.5 | moderately wet |
| −1 to 1 | near normal |
| −1.5 to −1 | moderately dry |
| −2 to −1.5 | severely dry |
| −2 or less | extremely dry |

The values are in the `fitted` element, a time series, so they can be used
like any other series. For example, the months of 2011 at the 12-month scale:

```{r}
window(spei12$fitted, start = c(2011, 1))
```

or the share of months in moderate or worse drought:

```{r}
mean(spei12$fitted <= -1, na.rm = TRUE)
```

`drought_events()` lists the drought events: the runs of consecutive months
with the index at or below -1. For each event it gives the first and the
last month, the duration in months, the severity (the sum of the index
values), the intensity (the severity divided by the duration) and the peak
(the lowest value) with its month:

```{r}
drought_events(spei12)
```

The 2011 drought started in May and was still going on at the end of the
series. The argument `threshold` changes the threshold, `type = "wet"` gives
the wet events, and `min.duration` drops the shortest events. See
`?drought_events` for the details.

`summary()` shows the call, the values and the fitted parameters of the
distribution for each calendar month, which are also in
`spei12$coefficients`.

## The SPI

The SPI is computed in the same way from precipitation alone. By default it
uses the Gamma distribution:

```{r, fig.alt = "Bar plot of SPI-12 at Wichita, 1980-2011"}
spi12 <- spi(wichita[, "PRCP"], 12)
plot(spi12, main = "Wichita, SPI-12")
```

The SPI and the SPEI often agree, but the SPEI also accounts for the effect
of temperature on the atmospheric water demand. Where temperatures are rising
or a dry period is also hot, the SPEI shows more severe drought than the SPI:

```{r, fig.alt = "Scatter plot of SPEI-12 against SPI-12 at Wichita, with the one-to-one line"}
plot(spi12$fitted, spei12$fitted,
  xlab = "SPI-12", ylab = "SPEI-12", asp = 1
)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
```

## Next steps

The functions have several options not covered here, such as the
distribution and fitting method, the reference period used to fit the
distribution, and weighting kernels. See `?spei` and `?spi` for details.
`spei()`, `spi()` and the PET functions also accept matrices and arrays, to
process several stations or a whole grid at once.
